stories.headline: Unemployment to surpass 5% and ‘things will get a bit harder’, treasurer Jim Chalmers warns
stories.claim: Australia's treasurer warns unemployment will top 5% and growth will stay below 2% in 2027 and 2028 ahead of the mid-year budget update.
stories.summary: Australians are being told to brace for a harder period, with unemployment expected to climb above 5% and growth held below 2% in both 2027 and 2028. Treasurer Jim Chalmers flagged the figures in parliament ahead of the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook next month. Inflation is forecast to ease only to the mid-3s percent by mid-2027 from 4.7% now, about a point above the May budget forecast. Unemployment already rose to 4.9% in October after five Reserve Bank rate hikes. AMP's chief economist Shane Oliver puts the chance of a more severe recession next year at 40%. Chalmers said the budget will include net savings to offset new spending, including extending a A$25 prescription medicine cap to the end of the decade at a cost of A$242m.
key_points: Chalmers says unemployment will climb above 5%, up from 4.9% in October, with growth slowing across 2027 and 2028.
Inflation is forecast to slow only to the mid-3s by mid-2027, about one percentage point above May budget expectations.
The mid-year budget update will include net savings to offset new spending, which Chalmers says will not slash essential services.
Shane Oliver of AMP warns growth could slump from 2.3% to below 1% and puts recession odds at 40%.
Official inflation data due Wednesday is likely to show inflation near 5%.
Bigger deficits are expected in later years as weaker growth feeds through to revenue and payments.
stories.market_take: Weaker growth and possible rate pressure could weigh on Australian equities and the Australian dollar.

stories.headline: Indonesia candy factory fire: rescuers recover more remains as 34 workers remain missing
stories.claim: Rescuers in Indonesia have recovered more remains from a Cikande candy factory fire, with 34 workers still missing.
stories.summary: Rescue teams in Indonesia have recovered more bodies from a candy factory fire in Cikande, Serang regency, Banten province on western Java, with 34 workers still unaccounted for, according to AP. The fire broke out on Saturday evening, killing three people and injuring four, while 15 people survived. Earlier reports put the number of missing workers at 36, believed to be trapped in parts of the damaged building, and firefighters were still cooling hotspots. The cause of the fire has not yet been announced. The disaster is likely to prompt scrutiny of workplace safety and fire regulations at Indonesian factories and small manufacturers.

34 workers are still missing, down from an earlier estimate of 36 as the search continues.

stories.headline: How AI is Accelerating Cyberattacks
stories.claim: Google says AI-driven autonomous hacking frameworks have reached a critical inflection point in cyberattacks.
stories.summary: Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say attackers are increasingly using autonomous AI agent frameworks to run multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. The report names open-source tools such as Cairn and PentAGI and says the trend has reached a critical inflection point. Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 found similar activity, including a Chinese-speaking group that used Cairn against more than a dozen organisations. Google also warns that LLM-generated exploits often do not work, adding to defenders' workload. The findings suggest AI is tilting the balance towards attackers, increasing demand for defensive security tools.

stories.headline: New 19-month low: Hong Kong stocks plunge as AI sell-off spreads to Asia
stories.claim: Hong Kong stocks hit a 19-month low on Monday as the US AI stock sell-off spread into Asia, with tech shares worst hit.
stories.summary: Hong Kong's stock market slid to its lowest level in 19 months on Monday, as a rout in US artificial intelligence shares spilled into Asia. The Hang Seng Tech Index fell as much as 3 per cent to below 3,400 points, leaving it down more than a third for the year. The morning session closed with the tech gauge down about 1.1 per cent, while the benchmark Hang Seng Index dropped as much as 1.8 per cent. The sell-off puts pressure on the city's large internet and technology groups and signals that investor nerves over AI valuations are now travelling across time zones. Whether the slide deepens will depend on how US AI stocks trade in the coming sessions.

stories.headline: San Francisco enjoys AI boom but economists warn a sharp AI correction could hit hard
stories.claim: San Francisco's AI-driven boom brings soaring rents and falling vacancies, but fears of a sharp AI share-price correction are growing.
stories.summary: San Francisco is enjoying an AI-powered revival, with soaring rents, falling office vacancies and a surge in local spending. Yet worries about a sharp correction in AI share prices are growing, especially after the IMF warned last month that such a fall was possible. The city is the centre of the boom, attracting around 60 per cent of US AI venture capital from 2023 to 2025, according to one study, and OpenAI and Anthropic are both based there. Anthropic recently listed on the Nasdaq, and Nvidia reported quarterly profits that doubled to $65bn (£49bn), even though its shares fell amid a scandal involving former chief Jensen Huang. Economists note that AI firms employ relatively few local workers, so direct job losses would be limited, but a downturn could ripple through restaurants, retail and services. City officials expect any slowdown to be a 'hiccup' rather than a major reversal, though the city remains about 35,000 jobs short of its pre-pandemic peak.

stories.headline: FTSE 100 caterer Compass plans to move main listing from London to New York
stories.claim: FTSE 100 caterer Compass is reportedly preparing to move its primary listing from London to New York, possibly announced with results on Tuesday.
stories.summary: Compass, the world's largest catering group and a FTSE 100 member worth about £43bn, is reportedly preparing to move its primary stock listing from London to New York. The plan could be announced alongside full-year results on Tuesday, according to the Financial Times and the Telegraph, though the switch itself is unlikely before 2028. Compass would keep a secondary listing in London and says the move reflects its US focus rather than problems with London liquidity. North America provides two-thirds of its revenue and three-quarters of its profit. If confirmed, it would be the second-largest exit from the London market in recent years after CRH left in April, following Flutter's departure in August. The move would add to government concern about companies leaving the City and is a blow to efforts to revive London's capital markets. Compass declined to comment, and shareholder consultation is planned.

stories.headline: Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out
stories.claim: NHS launches a 700,000-woman trial testing whether AI can help read breast cancer screening mammograms.
stories.summary: Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are being invited into what is described as the world's largest trial of artificial intelligence in breast cancer screening. The EDITH trial has started at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 NHS sites, and will run for around three years. Today two NHS specialists read each mammogram; in the trial one of those human readers will be replaced by AI, with AI either grading images before or reviewing them after experts see them. The £11m study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research and led by Warwick and Cambridge with NHS England, with four AI companies involved. Researchers say smaller studies show AI can raise detection rates, but they must confirm it does not cause unnecessary recalls or over-diagnosis of mild disease. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper backed the trial, saying safeguards are needed.
key_points: The EDITH trial will invite nearly 700,000 women aged 50 to 71 across the UK to take part in AI-assisted breast screening research.
Recruitment has begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites, and the study is expected to last about three years.
In one trial arm AI grades mammograms before human experts review them; in the other it reviews them afterwards.
The study is funded with £11m from the NIHR and led by the universities of Warwick and Cambridge with NHS England.
Researchers want to ensure AI does not increase unnecessary recalls or diagnose mild cancers that would never cause symptoms.
Breast cancer causes around 59,000 UK diagnoses a year, and the screening programme is estimated to prevent about 1,300 deaths annually.

stories.headline: US futures bounce as AI rout hits Asian stocks; Hong Kong hits 19-month low
stories.claim: US futures rose Monday as Asian markets stayed under pressure after last week's heavy tech and chip selloff.
stories.summary: US equity futures rose on Monday as investors bought the dip after a sharp slide in technology and chip shares, though gains were uneven. Nasdaq 100 futures climbed nearly 3% and S&P 500 futures rose about 2% in early trading, while South Korean shares fell about 4% before recovering some ground. The Nasdaq lost 10% last week, its worst weekly drop since March 2020, and Taiwan's benchmark posted its sharpest weekly fall since 1990. Investors are questioning whether heavy borrowing to fund AI data-centre spending can pay off quickly enough to support debt and high valuations. In response, Taiwan tightened short-selling rules, Chinese exchanges eased margin-financing requirements, and South Korea's finance minister was due to discuss a possible market stabilisation fund.

stories.headline: Tech suppliers raise AI server prices up to 45% months after deals are signed
stories.claim: Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are seeking higher prices on AI servers months after contracts were signed, as memory costs soar.
stories.summary: Major server makers are reportedly asking for higher prices on AI servers months after buyers have signed contracts, with increases of up to 45% in some cases. According to the Financial Times, Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are passing on sharply higher memory costs, with demands arriving as equipment is ready for delivery. JPMorgan research cited by the paper puts memory-cost increases above 400% since early 2024. One person quoted said GPU-server prices rose at least 20–30%, while CPU-node prices tripled or more. Trading firms including Jane Street, Optiver and Hudson River Trading have largely accepted the higher bills to secure capacity. XTX Markets alleges Dell sought an extra $62–70 million on a $549 million server deal despite a separate $5 million payment for price certainty. The dispute highlights how fixed-price AI infrastructure deals may not be as fixed as buyers assumed.

stories.headline: South Asian nations emerge as labour sources for Japan’s ageing farms
stories.claim: Bangladeshi workers are emerging as a new labour source for Japan's ageing farms as South-east Asian wages rise.
stories.summary: Bangladesh and Nepal are becoming an important source of farm labour for Japan, as wages rise in Vietnam and the Philippines and the flow of workers from those countries slows. Tokyo-based training firm Mirai, part of Sustainable Holdings, has placed its first two Bangladeshi candidates for farm work, with jobs at an agricultural company in Aomori prefecture. Japanese government data show Type 1 specified skilled foreign workers in agriculture rose 26% year on year to 44,050 in June. Indonesia remains the largest supplier with 18,255 workers, while Bangladesh's numbers jumped 127% to 334. The shift matters because farm labour shortages in Japan are chronic, driven by an ageing population.
key_points: Mirai has introduced its first Bangladeshi candidates for farm work after they passed Japan's specified skilled worker agriculture exam in August.
Type 1 agricultural workers reached 44,050 in June, up 26% from a year earlier, according to Japan's Immigration Services Agency.
Indonesia supplies the most workers (18,255, up 45%), while Nepal rose 30% to 916, Sri Lanka 60% to 638 and Bangladesh 127% to 334.
Wages rising in Vietnam, the Philippines and other South-east Asian countries are making those workers harder to attract.
Including Type 2 workers, the total in agriculture was 67,905 at the end of December 2025.
Sustainable Holdings offers free tuition at partner schools and helps with housing once workers arrive in Japan.

stories.headline: OpenAI chief scientist proposes industry-wide limits on powerful AI until safety monitoring improves
stories.claim: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed voluntary industry-wide limits on powerful AI until monitoring and safety milestones are met.
stories.summary: OpenAI's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, has called on AI developers to agree common limits on building increasingly powerful models until researchers can better understand and monitor them. In a blog post published on Sunday, 22 November, he suggested shared thresholds based partly on perplexity, a measure of how well a model predicts text, with developers committing not to cross them until monitoring and safety milestones are reached. He did not specify an initial limit or a start date, and warned that AI could drive fundamental training advances as early as 2027, potentially outpacing safety work. CEO Sam Altman endorsed the idea on X, calling it the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while. The proposal is voluntary rather than regulation, and it lands as US Democrats, who won sweeping midterm victories, prepare to push for tougher AI oversight, setting up a likely clash with President Trump, who has opposed broad AI restrictions.

stories.claim: Former PMs Theresa May and Tony Blair have warned Prime Minister Andy Burnham against rejoining the EU after his Brussels 'reset deal'.
stories.summary: Former prime ministers are warning Andy Burnham against seeking to rejoin the European Union. Theresa May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that she was 'aghast' he is considering it, saying 'Brexit is done' and that he wanted to 'pat people on the head'. Tony Blair said Britain should rejoin only if the EU reforms and embraces technology and innovation, calling Brexit 'a real mistake', while David Cameron said a rejoin conversation would be long and painful. Four of Britain's nine living ex-PMs have now spoken out. The comments follow Burnham's 'reset deal' struck at a Brussels summit on Friday, which gives 100,000 Europeans aged 18 to 31 the right to live, work and study in Britain for up to three years, aligns Britain with EU food and drink safety rules and links emissions trading. Burnham has floated the customs union, single market or a fresh referendum for informal long-term talks, but has ruled out major changes before the next general election, citing Labour's 2024 manifesto. Reform UK called the deal a betrayal, while Kemi Badenoch plans to attack it at a CBI speech and in parliament on Monday.

stories.headline: Unpaid taxes, outstanding payments, court orders: 400,000 Malaysians restricted from travelling
stories.claim: Malaysia says 404,848 citizens have faced immigration travel bans since 2024 over tax, court and debt issues.
stories.summary: Malaysia's Immigration Department says 404,848 Malaysians have been subject to travel restrictions since 2024, for reasons ranging from unpaid income tax and customs or EPF obligations to court orders, bankruptcy cases and unpaid student loans. Director-General Zakaria Shaaban said in an interview that the department acts on notices from other agencies and cannot take payments at checkpoints to lift a ban. Travellers must settle the matter directly with the agency that imposed the restriction, and the department updates its records only once that agency confirms. Zakaria also said the system helps catch people with active arrest warrants at border checks. He urged citizens to check their status online before travelling. The figures put a spotlight on how widely travel bans are used as a debt-collection tool in Malaysia.

stories.headline: Love made a fool of Beau Lamarre-Condon but did not make him a murderer, defence argues
stories.claim: Defence in the trial of ex-officer Beau Lamarre-Condon argues love, not murder, explains the 2024 Paddington shootings.
stories.summary: In a Sydney court, the defence for former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon has argued that he was a poorly behaved boyfriend, not a murderer, in the trial over the fatal shootings of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at Baird's Paddington home on 19 February 2024. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one of aggravated break and enter, claiming he acted in self-defence after Baird allegedly lunged at him with a knife. The prosecution, led by Brett Hatfield SC, says he developed a jealous obsession and shot both men, rejecting his account as a fabrication. The defence, led by John Stratton SC, says forensic gaps, including no blood on the trigger and an unlocated bullet, leave reasonable doubt. The jury must now decide the verdict in the New South Wales Supreme Court.

stories.claim: PM Andy Burnham will tell MPs on Tuesday that more essential services should be brought under public control.

stories.headline: India's Tata Steel moves to control APL Apollo with $1.67 billion stake buy, open offer
stories.claim: Tata Steel will buy a 26.38% stake in APL Apollo for about $1.67 billion and launch a mandatory open offer, gaining control.
stories.summary: Tata Steel is set to take control of India's largest structural steel tubes maker, APL Apollo, through a stake purchase worth about 155.11 billion rupees (US$1.67 billion). The deal, announced on Monday 23 November, covers an initial 26.38% stake at 2,100 rupees per share, a 1% discount to Friday's close. A mandatory open offer for a further 26% at 2,301.4 rupees per share, worth up to 167.56 billion rupees, follows. The move comes a day after APL Apollo agreed to buy Tata Steel's tubes business and its entire stake in Tata Steel Colors for up to 280 billion rupees in cash. Tata Steel says the combined downstream business will lift its share of downstream operations to about 53% from 35%. APL Apollo shares fell 10% and Tata Steel dropped 4% on the news.

Shares of APL Apollo fell 10% and Tata Steel fell 4% following the announcement.

stories.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Race to find survivors after Russian attack on apartment block kills at least nine
stories.claim: Russian strikes kill at least nine in Dymer, Ukraine, while a Russian warship sinks in Libya and Poland reports Russian missiles.
stories.summary: Rescuers in Ukraine were searching the rubble of a five-storey block of flats in Dymer, north of Kyiv, after a Russian strike killed at least nine people and left others missing. Across the Kyiv region and beyond, overnight attacks killed at least 12 people, including two in a Vyshneve supermarket. Separately, a Russian navy corvette, the Merkury, was severely damaged and sank in the Libyan port of Benghazi in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, more than 1,000 miles from Ukraine. In Poland, authorities say three objects that landed in the south-east were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, and Nato allies meet in Brussels on Monday. Denmark has expelled a Russian official over an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian American rapper, and is expected to press the EU for firmer action.

stories.headline: Flood risk to rise during northeast monsoon as high tides may coincide with heavy rain
stories.claim: Singapore's PUB warns flood risk rises through January 2027 as high tides coincide with northeast monsoon rain.
stories.summary: Singapore's national water agency, PUB, has warned that flood risks will rise until January 2027 during the northeast monsoon, when high tides may coincide with heavy rain. Low-lying coastal areas such as East Coast Park could see transient flooding, which has already been observed when tide levels exceed 3.3m even without rain. The first high-tide window is from 26 to 28 November, with the highest tides, up to about 3.5m, expected from 23 to 26 January 2027. PUB says flooding could be more widespread and severe if high tides coincide with heavy rainfall, as elevated seas restrict stormwater discharge. The agency links the growing risk to climate change, which is bringing more intense rainfall and rising sea levels.

stories.headline: Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
stories.claim: UK disability minister Stephen Timms to call for a fundamental overhaul of Pip assessments in review published Tuesday.
stories.summary: Disability minister Sir Stephen Timms says the personal independence payment (Pip) assessment process needs a 'fundamental overhaul', as his year-long review finds the system 'no longer fit for purpose'. The review, to be published in full on Tuesday, would introduce a fast-track process for people with the most severe conditions and end-of-life care. It follows a separate Milburn review that proposed moving under-25s off Pip. The cost of Pip is forecast to exceed £41bn by 2030, up from £15bn in 2020, with about 4 million claimants in the UK. Disability charities warn that changes must not weaken support, and it is still unclear how the two reviews will fit together.
key_points: Sir Stephen Timms's review says Pip assessments need a fundamental overhaul to better reflect people's varying costs and needs.
The review recommends a fast-track, less burdensome process for people with the most severe conditions and end-of-life care.

Republicans hold at least 173 seats. Four races remain uncalled, including contests in Minnesota and Tennessee, and two Louisiana seats go to a 12 December runoff, so the total could still shift slightly. The party's net gain of around 40 to 44 seats would be the third-largest in half a century, behind 2010 and 1994. Democrats also control the Senate, with a 56-seat majority, creating divided government under President Donald Trump. Voters cited high prices, the war with Iran and corruption concerns. Democrats plan a 100-day agenda on living costs, healthcare and immigration from January, including investigating the administration and blocking cabinet nominees, though Trump retains veto power over legislation.

Gordon Brothers froze about £50m of cash before releasing around £21m over two weeks, and it is weighing a break-up, which it says would better protect staff. Insiders accuse it of driving the business down for insolvency gains, which it denies. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds have pressed Gordon Brothers for answers.

stories.headline: Delta Atlanta flights delayed by weight-and-balance system failure

Staff used manual workarounds to dispatch aircraft while technicians restored the system, and the disruption reached flights across the US. The FAA said the Delta problem was unrelated to its own air traffic control systems. The incident comes a week after an FAA telecoms failure on 13 November caused a nationwide ground stop of over four hours and about 12,462 cancellations; the agency linked that outage to a router installation at a facility run by L3Harris and paused further installations. United Airlines also delayed departures after a separate outage of its own. stories.headline: Taiwan widens its short-selling ban after the Taiex’s worst week since 1991
stories.claim: Taiwan bans short selling below previous close and tightens margin rules after Taiex's worst week since 1991.
stories.summary: Taiwan's financial regulator has banned short selling of local stocks below the previous day's close, effective 23 November, after the Taiex suffered its worst week since 1991. The index fell 6.2% on Friday and lost almost 18% over the week. The Financial Supervisory Commission also raised the minimum margin for short sales to 150% from 130% and halted new put warrant listings. It is the third round of curbs this month, following earlier cuts to intraday short-selling limits and a ban for stocks that had fallen 3.5% or more. The sell-off has been driven by doubts over AI spending returns, worries about tighter US AI regulation and margin-financing risks, and the state-backed NT$500bn fund has been buying shares since 6 November.

stories.headline: The AI Build-Out Is Sucking Up Resources and Crowding Out the Rest of the Economy

Some analysts estimate Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia and Meta could spend as much as $1.4 trillion by 2027, while Gartner projects global AI spending will reach $2.5 trillion this year. Goldman Sachs economists warn AI could starve other productive sectors of capital, and Apollo's Torsten Slok expects hyperscaler capex to hit about 3% of GDP a year over 2027 to 2029, against 1.4% in 2025. AI took 65.4% of US venture-capital deal value in 2025, leaving sectors such as biotech under pressure. The piece argues that higher borrowing costs from competition for capital could also choke off other projects, making this a key macro risk.

stories.headline: Mexico captures FBI most-wanted cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro' in Sinaloa raid
stories.claim: Mexican forces captured alleged cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, 'El Chapo Isidro', on the FBI's most-wanted list, in a Sinaloa raid.
stories.summary: Mexico's military captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as 'El Chapo Isidro' and one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, in a special forces raid in Guasave, Sinaloa, on Friday night. The operation, which Mexico's defence ministry said had US intelligence support, triggered gunfights, burning vehicles and roadblocks across Sinaloa, though violence had largely subsided by Saturday. Two other alleged gang leaders, including his second-in-command, were arrested alongside him, and the three were flown to Mexico City to be handed to prosecutors. Security forces said seven attackers were killed and eight suspects arrested, while four Mexican soldiers died. Meza Flores was indicted in the US in 2012, carries a US$5m reward, and is accused of trafficking heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and fentanyl into the United States. Military released the first photographs of him after the arrest, and the capture is a significant blow to the Beltrán Leyva group, which is allied with one faction of the Sinaloa cartel.

stories.headline: Blair says UK should rejoin EU only if it reforms, especially on technology
stories.claim: Blair says the UK should rejoin the EU only on heavily conditioned terms, with EU reform and stronger UK tech innovation.
stories.summary: Sir Tony Blair has said Britain should rejoin the European Union only on heavily conditioned terms, arguing that the EU must reform and that Britain must be ready to walk away from talks. Speaking to The Sunday Times, he said Brexit was a real mistake but that the debate has changed since 2016, with technology innovation now central to the question. He warned that AI carries very considerable risks, that the EU may be moving in the wrong direction on tech, and that the UK lacks the dynamism of other countries in the sector. His remarks follow a deal Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed with Brussels, which he described as a win-win reset covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. A digital partnership on AI and quantum technology was also announced, with Ursula von der Leyen publicising it. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called the deal unfair, while Reform's Nigel Farage called it a betrayal of the British people. Burnham has ruled out discussing rejoining, and both sides plan an informal process on long-term options before the next UK-EU summit.

stories.claim: Satya Nadella says AI-discovered software flaws will make outages more likely and calls for tamper-proof AI oversight.
stories.summary: Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella warned that AI tools finding software flaws faster than companies can fix them will make outages more likely. Speaking at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, he apologised for a recent Outlook outage, which he said was a latent bug, and admitted Microsoft should have tested better and built firewalls to prevent a global failure. He said attackers now exploit vulnerabilities almost immediately, so patches must go straight to production, and that anyone can run a nation-state-level attack with AI. Nadella also outlined a 'trust architecture' with tamper-proof model logs, and said Microsoft's OpenAI deal gives it royalty-free access to a frontier model until 2032. He also said AI agents will reshape web advertising and payments.

stories.headline: Drone strike sets Russian cargo ship ablaze in Gulf of Finland; Helsinki warns war is spilling over
stories.claim: A drone strike set the Russian cargo ship Sparta II ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, and Finland says Ukraine was likely responsible.
stories.summary: A Russian cargo ship, the Sparta II, was set ablaze in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday after being hit by drones, and it later drifted into Finnish waters. Finland's armed forces and Border Guard point to Ukraine as likely responsible, though Kyiv has not commented and the reason for the attack is unclear. The vessel, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was sanctioned by the US and Ukraine and is reportedly suspected of carrying weapons from Syria to Russia. All 16 crew abandoned ship in lifeboats and were transferred to a nearby Russian vessel that is taking them home. Finland's defence minister said a Russian helicopter may have violated Finnish airspace during the rescue, and Helsinki introduced temporary aviation and maritime restrictions in the eastern Gulf. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said the war was spilling into the region, and the episode comes as Russian missiles and a drone crashed in Poland and NATO is due to meet in Brussels on Monday.

stories.headline: COP31 talks in Antalya stall over fossil fuel language as draft omits coal, oil and gas
stories.claim: COP31 talks in Antalya remain deadlocked over fossil fuel language as the latest draft again omits coal, oil and gas.
stories.summary: Negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, remained at odds over fossil fuels into a second day of overtime on Sunday, after talks were scheduled to end on Friday. The latest draft from the Turkish and Australian presidency again avoided naming coal, oil or gas, instead referring to the 2023 Dubai consensus on moving away from fossil fuels. About 130 countries, backed by the EU, want explicit phase-out language, while Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich states oppose it, and the EU has raised the prospect of 'no deal'. Other disputes include carbon capture and storage and a target for electricity to reach 35% of final energy by 2035. Developing nations are angry at the removal of a US$120 billion climate adaptation target, and some delegates have left, raising quorum concerns. Campaigners have labelled the summit the 'worst COP ever', noting that Berkeley Earth reported October 2026 was the warmest October on record.

stories.headline: Barnham villagers vote 94% to 'leave the UK' in symbolic poll against asylum plan
stories.claim: Residents of Barnham, Suffolk, voted 94% in a symbolic, non-binding poll to 'leave the UK' over plans to house asylum seekers at RAF Barnham.
stories.summary: Residents of the Suffolk village of Barnham voted 257 to 16 in a symbolic, non-binding poll on Saturday, with 94% of participants backing leaving the UK in protest at government plans to house up to 931 single male asylum seekers at the former RAF Barnham site. The vote has no legal force, as there is no mechanism for a village to leave the UK, and the village plans to call itself the 'Bailiwick of Barnham' and has unveiled its own flag. The Home Office has awarded a £3.4m design contract to Kier for the site, which could use a fast-track planning route, but said no final decision has been taken and that it is listening to local concerns. The council estimated around 500 people could vote, as it cannot use the electoral register. Barnham is the second village after Piddington in Oxfordshire to hold such a poll, where 285 of 312 voters backed leaving in September. Reform UK's Zia Yusuf attended the result, and Barnham's Labour MP Peter Prinsley said he will raise the opposition with the immigration minister this week. The plans are part of the government's effort to end hotel use for asylum seekers by 2029.
key_points: Barnham residents voted 257 to 16, or 94%, to leave the UK in a symbolic, non-binding poll on Saturday.
The vote protests government plans to house up to 931 single male asylum seekers at RAF Barnham.
The village plans to call itself the 'Bailiwick of Barnham' and has unveiled its own flag.
The Home Office says no final decision has been taken and that it is listening to local concerns; Kier has a £3.4m design contract.
Piddington in Oxfordshire held a similar vote in September, returning 285 votes to leave out of 312.

stories.headline: BepiColombo spacecraft enter orbit around Mercury
stories.claim: Two BepiColombo spacecraft have entered orbit around Mercury, only the second mission ever to do so.
stories.summary: The joint European-Japanese BepiColombo mission has entered orbit around Mercury, becoming only the second spacecraft ever to circle the smallest planet and the one closest to the Sun. The craft had travelled more than eight years and about 6bn miles to reach the planet, and flight controllers had planned to fire thrusters to achieve orbit. In early December the spacecraft will separate into a European orbiter and a Japanese orbiter. Science operations are due to begin in April next year, and the orbiters should last about three years before running out of fuel. The €1.6bn (£1.4bn) mission aims to explain how Mercury formed so close to the Sun, why it has a magnetic field, and what ice lies in its permanently shadowed craters.

stories.claim: India's Congress youth wing vows more protests against Meta after office clashes over restricted accounts.
stories.summary: The youth wing of India's main opposition Congress party has warned of more protests against Meta after supporters stormed the company's Hyderabad office, smashed plants and clashed with police. Workers also spray-painted anti-Meta slogans outside the Mumbai office, and the group threatened to 'storm your offices across the country' unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders are restored. The dispute centres on Meta's removal of content in India, where thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and critics of the government remain restricted. Meta says it restricts content to comply with local laws, and disclosures show it restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in all of 2025. India's government says takedowns only target content that breaches local law or threatens public safety, and it has ordered removals within three hours. Meta declined to comment, and India's IT ministry did not respond.
key_points: The Indian Youth Congress clashed with police after storming Meta's Hyderabad office on Friday, and sprayed anti-Meta slogans outside the Mumbai office.
The group has warned of further protests across the country unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders are restored.
Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025.
India's government ordered platforms in February to remove unlawful content within three hours, down from 36 hours.
Meta declined to comment, and the IT ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
Free speech groups and Reporters Without Borders say removals of journalistic content are rising in India.
stories.market_take: Mostly a regulatory and reputational issue for Meta in its largest market by users, with little immediate financial effect.

stories.headline: Anthropic's record IPO is followed by an AI-led tech rout that pushes US indexes into correction
stories.claim: Anthropic shares fell about 9% on their second day of trading, as an AI-led rout pushed the S&P 500 and Dow into correction.
stories.summary: Anthropic's record IPO has been overshadowed by a sharp AI-led tech sell-off that pushed the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory. The S&P 500 closed at 6,918.45 on Friday, down 3.59%, its seventh straight losing session and its longest such run since February 2020, while the Nasdaq erased all of its 2026 gains. Chipmakers led the drop, with Micron, Broadcom, Nvidia and AMD down roughly 12% to 14%, and the VIX topped 30 for the first time since March. Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $83 in Thursday's IPO, raising about $81 billion, and opened at $111.50 before closing at $97.17 on debut, then fell about 9% on Friday to roughly $85 by midday. Retail investors bought more than $750 million of the stock on debut, a record for a debut according to Vanda Research. Investor concerns include the debt-funded AI spending boom, Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia chief executive, and a Democratic sweep in the midterms that raised fears of tighter AI regulation. Asian markets were hit hard, with Taiwan's index falling 5.65% in its steepest weekly drop since 1997 and the Nikkei and Kospi each down about 5%, and Taiwan has widened short-sale curbs. Markets reportedly price a high chance of a US rate rise in December, and senator Adam Schiff has urged Congress to rule out a taxpayer bailout for AI.

The Dow entered correction territory and the Nasdaq erased all of its 2026 gains.

Taiwan's index fell 5.65% in its steepest weekly drop since 1997, prompting wider short-sale curbs and state share buying.
Investors are questioning the returns on debt-funded AI spending, following Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO.

stories.headline: ICE arrests at Seattle airport spark outrage from officials and politicians
stories.claim: Masked ICE agents detained two passengers on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma airport, drawing condemnation from the Port of Seattle and Governor Bob Ferguson.
stories.summary: Federal immigration agents detained two passengers on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning, just before an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles was due to leave. Video of the arrest shows a woman forced to the ground, and the Port of Seattle and Washington's Democratic governor, Bob Ferguson, condemned the episode. ICE says the two detained passengers, identified by their lawyer as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and Sofia Hernandez Mejia, are Mexican nationals who overstayed their visas. DHS says the daughter threw hot coffee at officers and faces a charge of assaulting a federal officer, while the lawyer says neither has a criminal history and that the agents wore plain clothes without identification. Alaska Airlines and the Port say they had no advance notice of the operation, and the airline is reviewing its protocols. Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, have promised oversight of ICE tactics, adding pressure to the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

stories.headline: The Outages Are Just Getting Started

The total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 has passed 100,000, against about 25,000 in 2022. Only about 300 flaws are on the US CISA exploited list this year, while VulnCheck counts 1,500 known exploited vulnerabilities.

stories.headline: NASA Mars rover and orbiter suffer glitches
stories.claim: NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter may be nearing end of life after a reaction wheel fault, while Perseverance rover is paused by radio problems.
stories.summary: NASA is grappling with two problems at once on Mars. The 2001 Mars Odyssey orbiter, which has been operating for a quarter of a century, dropped into safe mode between 4 and 6 November because one of its remaining reaction wheels stopped spinning. Engineers got the wheel moving again, but if its thrusters must be used, only a few months of fuel remain, putting the mission at risk. Separately, the Perseverance rover's primary radio failed on 30 October and its backup was running at roughly half its expected power, so science work is on hold while it relies on a slower X-band link. Odyssey relays data for several Mars missions, so its loss would be keenly felt, though ESA's Mars Express and Trace Gas Orbiter could take on some of the load.

The wheel responded when commanded, but only a few months of thruster fuel remain if it is needed.
Odyssey has relayed images from Phoenix and the Spirit, Opportunity and Curiosity rovers, and is part of NASA's Mars Relay Network.
Perseverance's primary radio and backup both deemed inoperable after a 30 October fault, so the rover uses a slower X-band link.
Engineers are first trying to restore the backup radio, then will address the primary.
ESA's Mars Express and Trace Gas Orbiter could cover some relay work if Odyssey is lost.

stories.headline: Lean verifies Anthropic claim that Claude helped prove the Riemann hypothesis
stories.claim: Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative say they independently verified the Lean code behind Anthropic's claimed Riemann hypothesis proof, though the proof is not yet accepted.
stories.summary: The Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative said on Saturday they had independently verified a proof of the Riemann hypothesis by checking the Lean code published by Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge, and expressed full confidence in its correctness. Alpöge, who said he worked with a non-public version of Claude over about six weeks, first made the claim on Friday, a day after Anthropic's record Nasdaq debut, and acknowledged the timing was awkward. Several Zulip participants, including Andrew Sutherland of MIT, said the code compiles, though Terence Tao said human verification will take time. The complete argument reportedly runs to more than 250,000 pages and lacks a readable human explanation. Under Clay Institute rules a solution needs peer review and two years of scrutiny before the $1 million prize is paid, and Stanford's Ravi Vakil had earlier posted a human-written draft of the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis that was later flagged for problems.

stories.headline: Burnham seals UK-EU reset deals on trade, emissions and youth mobility, with student fees unresolved
stories.claim: Andy Burnham sealed UK-EU reset deals on food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility, while student fees remain unresolved.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU agreed three deals at a Brussels summit on Friday covering food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which he called the biggest step in UK-EU ties since Brexit. The youth scheme lets up to 100,000 18-to-31-year-olds from each side live, work and study in the other for up to three years, double Britain's initial 50,000 offer. The food deal would remove most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU rules from 2028, and the emissions trading systems would be linked, shielding UK exporters from EU carbon border levies. The government estimates the package adds 0.5% to GDP, about £17bn a year, a figure a Treasury analysis and independent economists dispute. The EU says the agreements will not take effect until tuition fees for EU students in British universities are settled, with a six-month deadline; London has reportedly offered £12,000 against up to £38,000 now. Legislation is due in Parliament next week, and Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch have attacked the deal, with the Conservatives vowing to scrap it.

The youth scheme allows up to 100,000 18-to-31-year-olds from each side to live, work and study in the other for up to three years.
The EU says the deals will not take effect without equal tuition fees for EU students, with a six-month deadline; the fees row is unresolved.
The government says the package adds 0.5% to GDP (about £17bn), which the Treasury analysis and critics dispute.
The Conservatives estimate a £281 annual cost per household and vow to scrap the emissions trading agreement.
Legislation is due in Parliament next week, and MPs will vote on the reset deal this week.

stories.claim: JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon vows to claw back the cost of the UK's temporarily doubled bank surcharge, which he calls unfair.
stories.summary: JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon has vowed the bank will look for ways to offset the cost of the UK's temporarily doubled bank surcharge, calling the measure unfair. Speaking at a London event on Thursday, he said JPMorgan would set an example so governments understand the trade-offs of such penalties, though he gave no specifics. Chancellor John Healey announced in his October Budget that the surcharge on bank profits above £100m would rise from 3 to 6 per cent for a 15-month period, with the increase taking effect in January, to help fund energy bill support. JPMorgan expects to pay between £100m and £150m more because of the change, while the Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts about £1.5bn in extra revenue but warns around £190m of profits could leave the UK. The dispute also puts the bank's planned £3bn Canary Wharf headquarters under scrutiny, as the bank has previously suggested it could scrap the project. With the 25% corporation tax rate plus the surcharge, the biggest UK banks face a total rate of 31%.

stories.headline: Amazon campaigns against NYC delivery bill backed by Mamdani
stories.claim: Amazon is escalating its campaign against New York City's Delivery Protection Act, now placing warnings of up to $5 per order on shipping labels.
stories.summary: Amazon has escalated its campaign against New York City's Delivery Protection Act by printing warnings on shipping labels that the Council could add up to $5 to each Amazon order. The labels follow app and website notices shown earlier in the week. The bill, introduced by Councilmember Tiffany Cabán and backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, would require last-mile delivery firms to hire drivers as full-time employees and obtain city licences for their facilities. Amazon says it would close its 15 last-mile sites in the city and cut about 2,000 jobs, and an Amazon-commissioned study estimates delivery costs would rise by about $664 a year per New Yorker, or roughly $5.20 per package. Labour unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have accused the company of intimidation and greed, pointing to its market value of nearly $3 trillion. Queens councilman Phil Wong reportedly withdrew his co-sponsorship in September, though the bill still has 35 co-sponsors and supporters say it retains momentum. New York would be the first US city to adopt such rules.

stories.headline: Vietnam passes law to speed land clearance for priority projects
stories.claim: Vietnam's National Assembly approved a revised land law letting authorities speed site clearance for priority projects before compensation plans are finalised.
stories.summary: Vietnam's National Assembly approved a revised land law on Saturday, 21 November, with 474 votes in favour from 479 deputies, allowing site clearance to begin before compensation plans are approved. The fast-track covers nationally important projects, urgent public investment, and cases where more than 75% of affected landholders consent, provided no resettlement is needed and plans are publicly disclosed. The revision also overhauls land pricing to make valuations more data-driven and transparent, gives local governments more power over pricing and compensation, and plans a digital land database. Officials say it adds protections such as stronger resettlement rights, up to three years of livelihood support and expanded vocational training. The aim is to unblock property and infrastructure projects that have stalled over compensation disputes as Vietnam targets growth of at least 10% in 2026 and high-income status by 2045. Critics warn it may weaken safeguards and reduce farmers' leverage in a country where land disputes sometimes spark protests. The law takes effect on 1 July 2027, with new pricing rules from 1 January 2028, and parliament also passed revised housing and real estate business laws.
key_points: Parliament approved the revised land law on 21 November with 474 votes in favour, five against and eight abstaining.
Expropriation decisions can precede approval of compensation plans for priority projects or where 75% of landholders consent.

stories.claim: Hackers leaked files they say were stolen from vendors of JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard; the records are unverified and card numbers appear not exposed.
stories.summary: Hackers have published files they claim were stolen from third-party service providers working for JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard, exposing mainly marketing data on customers. Reuters found more than 16,000 Chase customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, plus 124 apparently belonging to bank staff, though it could not verify the records. The extortion group n0n claimed the attack on 16 November and responsibility for the leak. Visa said the breach involved a provider in Asia-Pacific and that card numbers were not exposed, while Mastercard said emails from one benefits programme were affected. SOCRadar later found the 14 published files contain no card numbers, CVVs, passwords or home addresses, but could enable phishing through mobile numbers and booking details. The published files are only about 0.4% of the roughly 4.3 GB n0n claims to hold, so further releases are possible. None of the companies has named the vendors, and all say their main payment systems were unaffected.

stories.headline: UN Geneva talks fail to agree binding rules on killer robots, deferring to 2028
stories.claim: UN Geneva talks on killer robots ended without a binding treaty mandate, deferring work on an instrument to a 2028 meeting.
stories.summary: UN talks in Geneva on lethal autonomous weapons collapsed at about 5am on Saturday without a mandate for a legally binding treaty. All 128 states under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons agreed instead to develop an international instrument over two years, reporting to a 2028 meeting. Russia objected to the agenda on the first day and blocked formal negotiations, and under the consensus rule its objections shaped a much weaker outcome. The US, UK, France, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Turkey and Israel were named by EU diplomats as resisting binding rules, with the US proposing a five-year window for non-binding guidelines. More than 100 states had wanted a new law, and a bloc led by Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama pushed for a treaty within a year. The International Committee of the Red Cross and UN chief António Guterres want a binding instrument, and campaigners called the result a missed opportunity, warning that it may soon be too late to regulate such weapons.

stories.headline: New open model Inkling 2 Mini thinks in loops to solve problems with fewer words and still runs on a laptop
stories.claim: Thinking Machines releases open model Inkling 2 Mini, which loops layers to reason longer and runs on a laptop.
stories.summary: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight model that reasons by re-running part of its network rather than generating more text. It runs 12 of its 24 layers three times per token, giving it 26.4 billion parameters in total with 5.4 billion active per token. The model handles text and images, offers a 1-million-token context window and is licensed under Apache 2.0. The company says it leads open models under 100 billion parameters on agentic coding tests, scoring 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5% on the Vals Index v2.2. Artificial Analysis rates it 20 on its Intelligence Index, level with Qwen3.8 27B, at roughly six times lower cost and four times the speed. It runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of memory and on Nvidia's DGX Spark, which matters for developers wanting capable models offline.

stories.headline: What do UN votes tell us about the new world order?

The vote is non-binding, but it could change the maps used by institutions worldwide. Critics of the Mercator projection argue that it makes Africa look similar in size to Greenland, when it is roughly 14 times larger. The African Union adopted the Equal Earth projection in February, and the US has faced criticism over an earlier mislabelling of countries on a map of Africa.

stories.headline: The Penny Is Dead. Now It’s Official.
stories.claim: President Trump signed the Common Cents Act into law, formally ending penny production in the US.
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has signed the bipartisan Common Cents Act, which formally ends the minting of the one-cent coin after nearly 250 years. Both the House and Senate passed the measure by voice vote, and the Mint stopped making pennies in November 2025. The penny remains legal tender, and the Federal Reserve will keep recirculating the roughly 114 billion pennies in circulation. The law also lets businesses that take cash round prices to the nearest 5 cents and allows the nickel to be made with a zinc core. Supporters say it will save about $85m a year, against the Mint's earlier estimate of $56m in immediate annual savings.

The context window is the model's working memory, and it has grown roughly 120-fold since GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens. The finding matters for companies paying for AI compute, since it suggests cheaper retrieval-based methods can match brute-force long inputs in many cases.

stories.headline: Jury convicts Jonathan Rinderknecht of arson over deadly January 2025 Palisades fire
stories.claim: A federal jury in Los Angeles convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht of arson over the deadly January 2025 Palisades fire; sentencing is set for 17 March.
stories.summary: A federal jury in Los Angeles on Friday convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of two federal counts, destruction of property by fire and arson, over the Palisades fire. Prosecutors say he lit a fire on 1 January 2025 that smouldered in root systems before flaring again on 7 January and becoming the Palisades Fire, one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history. The blaze killed 12 people, destroyed more than 6,800 buildings and caused damage estimated at about $150bn (£114bn). His first trial in June ended in a 10-2 deadlock in favour of acquittal, so prosecutors narrowed the charges and retried the case. The second time, they relied on phone-tower and iPhone location data, photographs of his car, fire-camera images, security footage and testimony from Uber passengers and his girlfriend, and ruled out fireworks as an alternative source. Each count carries five to 20 years, and sentencing is set for 17 March. His lawyer says he was wrongly accused and the defence respects the jury's decision.
key_points: A federal jury convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, on Friday of arson and destruction of property by fire over the Palisades fire.
The fire he allegedly started on 1 January 2025 flared again on 7 January and became the Palisades Fire.

stories.headline: US judge approves Bayer's $7.25bn Roundup cancer settlement
stories.claim: A Missouri judge gave final approval to Bayer's $7.25bn Roundup cancer settlement, which covers current and future non-Hodgkin lymphoma claims.
stories.summary: A Missouri state judge in St Louis, Timothy Boyer, has given final approval to Bayer's $7.25bn nationwide class settlement resolving claims that Roundup weedkiller causes cancer. Judge Boyer called the deal fair, reasonable and adequate, and overruled objections that individual payouts would be too low. Payments will range from about $10,000 to $165,000 depending on exposure, age at diagnosis and illness severity, and Bayer will fund the deal through annual payments over up to 21 years, including $600 million in attorneys' fees. The settlement covers people already diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who develop it later, and Bayer faced about 65,000 claims. The approval follows a June 7-2 US Supreme Court ruling that federal pesticide law overrides state failure-to-warn claims. Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer and says the deal contains no admission of liability, called the approval a decisive milestone in managing its litigation risk. The judge stressed that delay could leave victims, some with terminal cancer, waiting an indeterminate number of years. The approval can still be appealed, which would pause payments until challenges are resolved.
key_points: Judge Timothy Boyer of a St Louis state court gave final approval to Bayer's $7.25bn Roundup settlement, calling it fair, reasonable and adequate.
The deal covers people already diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma as well as those who develop it in future, and aims to resolve nearly all current and future Roundup claims in the US.
Individual payments range from about $10,000 to $165,000, depending on exposure, age at diagnosis and severity of illness.
Bayer will fund the settlement through annual payments over up to 21 years, and the deal includes $600 million in attorneys' fees.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang affair and Alice Huang chip-smuggling probe roil Nvidia; Bessent leaves door open to return
stories.claim: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says he would not oppose Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia CEO, softening his earlier stance.
stories.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CBS on Sunday that he would not oppose Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia's chief executive, a notable softening from his call a week earlier for the board to hire an outsider. Bessent said the administration still lacked answers on Nvidia's advanced AI chip sales to China and wanted to know where responsibility lies before endorsing any return, and he gave the company 10 days to respond. The shift comes after Huang admitted in an email to staff that he had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based tech executive whom US intelligence has reportedly linked to a Chinese espionage network. Huang resigned as CEO on 12 November, and the board accepted the resignation on 17 November, saying he is not coming back and that it has launched an independent investigation into corporate security and possible intellectual property leakage. President Trump and Elon Musk have reportedly backed his reinstatement, and Colette Kress is interim chief executive. Congressional committees and federal prosecutors are also examining whether illicit chip sales lifted revenue, with Singapore-based Megaspeed under review as a possible front company. The scandal has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars off Nvidia's market value, and the company is reportedly due to report quarterly results next week.

Bessent had earlier urged the board to look outside for leadership and accused Nvidia of a 'culture of non-compliance'.

stories.headline: Signal blocks screenshots and AI agents from reading private chats
stories.claim: Signal now blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and triggers protections on Android to stop AI assistants like Siri and Gemini from reading private chats.
stories.summary: Signal has begun restricting screenshots to stop AI assistants from reading private conversations. On iOS 27 it blocks screenshots outright, and on supported Android versions it triggers protection when an AI assistant tries to access the screen, blocking Siri, Gemini and other agents by default. Users can switch the protection off in settings. CEO Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that operating-system AI, such as Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence, poses an existential threat to privacy, because agents can use optical character recognition to pull decrypted messages from the screen and send them to cloud servers. The move follows Meta's AI agent Muse capturing Signal content on Android and macOS through broad permissions that users granted, according to Meta. Signal admits screenshot blocking is only a partial fix, because agents can still reach app data through the file system, and it cannot yet offer the same protection on macOS. Signal already blocks Microsoft's Recall on Windows and is urging Apple, Google and Microsoft to let apps block AI agents entirely. Apple's macOS 27.3, now in public beta, adds stricter permission prompts.

Signal's apps now block Siri, Gemini and other AI agents by default, though users can turn the protection off.

stories.headline: Honda, Toyota recall 1.6m vehicles over Takata airbag rupture risk
stories.claim: Honda and Toyota are recalling about 1.6 million vehicles in the US over Takata airbag inflator rupture risk.
stories.summary: Honda and Toyota are recalling about 1.6 million vehicles over the risk that Takata airbag inflators could rupture. Neither company has recorded an injury or crash linked to the vehicles, and no inflator has ruptured. The replacement inflators contain a moisture-absorbing material, unlike earlier recalled units, and parts are expected by early 2027. The Takata problem has caused at least 28 deaths in the US and more than 400 injuries since 2009, making it the largest auto recall in US history. The US regulator NHTSA said independent testing allowed the automakers to act before risks materialised. Toyota's recall includes 790,000 vehicles worldwide, of which 314,000 are in the US.

stories.headline: Russia unleashes barrage of missiles on Ukraine, killing at least 8
stories.claim: Russia launched a large missile and drone barrage on Ukraine, killing at least eight people and hitting Kyiv's bridges and power grid.

UNICEF also said at least 1,144 children were killed or wounded from January to October.

stories.headline: Dutch privacy watchdog warns consumers against buying AI smart glasses
stories.claim: Dutch privacy regulator AP advises consumers not to buy AI smart glasses after tests of six models found unsafe AI advice and security flaws.
stories.summary: The Dutch Data Protection Authority, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens, has advised consumers not to buy AI-powered smart glasses after testing six models sold in the Netherlands. Testers found the AI assistants gave dating advice to an adult who showed interest in a minor, falsely said emergency services were on the way during a CPR simulation, and misread medication leaflets. Some glasses also had security flaws that could let nearby devices connect, view recordings or operate the camera remotely. Recording indicator lights were dim and in some cases could be covered while the device kept recording. The regulator also said AI processing relies mostly on servers outside the EU and that users lacked clear information on data handling. Prices of the models ranged from under €100 to over €500, and the regulator did not name the products or call for a ban. It urged European politicians to take the findings into account when shaping AI policy, and the warning adds pressure on makers such as Meta, which has recently released a camera-free version.

stories.headline: BBC investigation: $811m-fined bail firm's scams continued through linked companies
stories.claim: A BBC investigation finds bail firms tied to Libre by Nexus kept taking money from detained migrants after the $811m fine.
stories.summary: A BBC investigation has found that Libre by Nexus, once America's largest immigration bail firm, kept operating through interconnected companies even after it was fined $811m in 2024 for scamming clients. Mildred Juarez, held in a Texas detention centre, said she paid $2,600 to Libre Immigration Services, which the BBC says is owned by a convicted fraudster, and waited weeks for a release that never came until another bail agent freed her after her friends paid more. Federal regulators said the firm implied GPS ankle monitors were court-mandated when they were its own requirement. The firm's co-founders had prior fraud and forgery convictions, and the company enabled more than 20,000 releases and took in over $230m in revenue across a decade. The company's spokesperson disputed the account, saying it only connects clients to licensed bondsmen. The report lands as ICE arrests have passed 1.2 million under Trump, driving demand for bail bonds and exposing migrants to exploitation; the White House and Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC.

stories.headline: Cincinnati Zoo hippo Fiona dies after swallowing child's hat
stories.claim: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's Nile hippo, died on 19 November after swallowing a knit hat that a ceiling fan blew into her enclosure.
stories.summary: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's Nile hippopotamus and a social media favourite since a premature birth in 2017, died on Thursday 19 November after swallowing a woollen hat. A visitor tossed the hat into the habitat, where a ceiling fan carried it through a small opening above the viewing windows. Staff tried several treatments, including endoscopy and a vibration plate meant to move the hat through her digestive tract, but the hat lodged far down her small intestine. Laparoscopic removal was judged impossible given its location, and surgery was considered too risky for an animal of her size. A necropsy found the hat about 25 feet beyond her final stomach compartment and confirmed that supportive care would not have worked. The US Senate adopted a resolution honouring her on Friday, and buildings were lit purple in tribute. The zoo's other hippos, Bibi, Tucker and Fritz, are eating and behaving normally.

stories.headline: Lubdub’s waterproof ECG patch is heading into a clinical trial in Australia
stories.claim: Australian startup Lubdub begins clinical trial of RMIT-invented waterproof wireless heart monitor patch in Perth.
stories.summary: A gel-free, waterproof wireless heart patch invented at RMIT University has moved from the lab into a clinical trial in Western Australia. The trial began this week at Midlands Medical Specialists in Perth, where patients already prescribed a traditional Holter monitor will wear the prototype alongside it. The patch can track heart rhythm continuously for up to 14 days, and RMIT says its data was 18 times cleaner than Holter readings in earlier testing. Australian startup Lubdub, co-founded by RMIT professor Sharath Sriram, says the device could let staff monitor up to 85 per cent more patients. The trial will generate evidence for possible regulatory approval, and the patch is the first of three planned heart technologies on one software platform.

stories.headline: Bobby Ray Inman, Intelligence Official Under Carter and Reagan, Dies at 95
stories.claim: Former NSA director and naval intelligence chief Bobby Ray Inman has died aged 95 in Austin, Texas.
stories.summary: Bobby Ray Inman, a former admiral who led US naval intelligence and the National Security Agency, died on Thursday in a hospital in Austin, Texas, aged 95. His son Thomas confirmed the death. Inman ran naval intelligence from 1974 to 1976 and became NSA director in July 1977 under President Jimmy Carter, a year after a Senate committee found the agency had improperly conducted domestic surveillance. He backed the 1978 Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which required court approval for intercepting international communications involving people in the US. He also later served in the Reagan administration and turned down a nomination by Bill Clinton to be defence secretary. No cause of death has been given.

stories.headline: Would A Staggered Age Of Consent Protect Women And Girls?
stories.claim: UK government is considering a staggered age of consent, backed by campaigners and Mia Latter, amid debate on protecting girls.
stories.summary: The UK government says it is considering changing the law to introduce a staggered age of consent, which would allow 16 and 17-year-olds to have sex with people close to their own age but make sex with much older adults illegal. The proposal is backed by campaigners and by Mia Latter, who has waived anonymity to describe a relationship with Russell Brand when she was 16 and he was 30, an account he denies. The columnist argues the change is a step forward but not a solution, noting police record about 204 rapes a day in England and Wales and that fewer than 3% of reported rapes lead to charges. The piece calls for better education, court reform and action on the wider culture, marking a year since the government's 10-year VAWG strategy.

stories.claim: Ganni is closing its Tmall flagship in China from 21 November 2026, ending its direct online retail presence there after four years.

The move contrasts with other Scandinavian labels such as Acne Studios, which is opening in Shanghai.

stories.headline: What Happened to Fashion’s Living Wage Commitments?
stories.claim: Clean Clothes Campaign's Fashion Checker finds most brands still fail to disclose wages or show living wage progress.
stories.summary: Only 3 percent of the 110 fashion brands assessed by the Clean Clothes Campaign disclose wage levels at their supplier factories, despite 41 percent publishing facility data. The seventh edition of its Fashion Checker, released for Living Wage Action Day, found that 32 percent have a living wage commitment but just 4 percent report tangible progress towards it. Benetton, Levi's, Adidas, Uniqlo and H&M received the lowest possible living wage score. Worker surveys found pay gaps of 73 percent in Bangladesh, 74 percent in Pakistan, 63 percent in Serbia and 66 percent in Turkey against living wage benchmarks. A quarter of assessed brands have no public grievance mechanism. The findings matter ahead of the EU's amended due diligence directive, which applies from 26 July 2029.

stories.claim: Polling by Fortius Global finds voters in 4 in 5 UK seats now back rejoining the EU.
stories.summary: A Fortius Global constituency model, based on a survey of more than 7,000 people taken this month, suggests that 512 of Great Britain's seats now favour rejoining the EU, against 73 for staying out and 47 too close to call. Voters in 274 of the 394 seats that backed Leave in 2016 now want to rejoin, including Kemi Badenoch's North West Essex, predicted at 59.4% in favour. The modelling also projects Labour would gain seats under closer EU ties, rising from about 370 under current arrangements to 475 under full membership. The firm was founded by former Obama pollster Jim Messina and worked for the Remain campaign in 2016, which the article notes as relevant context. The findings would strengthen Andy Burnham's push to open a debate on rejoining the EU, though some Labour MPs in Leave-voting seats are nervous.

stories.headline: Indian Man Sentenced to Almost 20 Years in Murder-for-Hire Plot on U.S. Soil
stories.claim: A US federal judge sentenced Indian national Nikhil Gupta to 235 months in prison for a murder-for-hire plot against Sikh leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
stories.summary: A US federal judge in Manhattan has sentenced Indian national Nikhil Gupta to 235 months, just over 19 years, for plotting to murder Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a Sikh separatist leader and US citizen. Gupta pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy and money laundering charges. US prosecutors allege he was directed by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, who supplied details of Pannun's New York address and daily routine. The 'hitman' Gupta was put in touch with was an undercover DEA officer. India has denied any involvement, and says Yadav is no longer employed by the government and that it set up an inquiry. The judge said Gupta will likely be deported after serving his sentence. The case remains a sharp point of tension between Washington and New Delhi.

stories.headline: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
stories.claim: Survivors describe the violence that drove Rohingya to flee Myanmar in 2017, following a recent ICJ genocide ruling.
stories.summary: Rohingya refugees who fled Myanmar in 2017 describe rivers running red with blood, burning villages and mass killings, as the International Court of Justice this week ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the group. The court said that killing people trying to escape was part of an effort to destroy the Rohingya as a people, not just ethnic cleansing. More than 700,000 people crossed into Bangladesh in 2017 and now live in what is the world's largest refugee camp. Many remain there almost a decade later, unable to work, study or leave the camps. The ruling comes as hundreds have died at sea this year and countries including Malaysia and India have discussed returning Rohingya to Myanmar. Campaigners hope the judgment will strengthen their case.

stories.headline: Congress Proxy-Voting Found Unconstitutional by Fifth Circuit
stories.claim: Full Fifth Circuit rules House proxy voting during Covid was unconstitutional, opening challenges to fiscal 2023 spending law.
stories.summary: The full Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans has ruled that House proxy voting during the Covid-19 pandemic violated the US Constitution's Quorum Clause. Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote the majority opinion, holding that members must be physically present for quorum. The ruling is narrow in scope, applying only to Texas's challenge to the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, which was part of the fiscal 2023 spending package. However, it could invite further challenges to parts of that multi-trillion-dollar package. Judge James Graves Jr. dissented, questioning why the remedy would be limited to a single provision. The decision is almost certain to be appealed to the US Supreme Court.

The Houthis have threatened Saudi Red Sea ports, warned airlines off Saudi airspace and claimed attacks on a power station and port in the south. The fighting, which reignited in July, is unfolding alongside the US-led war against Iran and has deepened Yemen's humanitarian crisis.

stories.headline: Half a Million Containers Hang on 250 Watchmen as LA/LB Port Strike Threat Looms
stories.claim: A possible strike by about 250 port watchmen could shut much of the LA and Long Beach port complex from Saturday.
stories.summary: A strike by around 250 port watchmen could shut much of the US's busiest container gateway from 12:01am Pacific time on Saturday, with more than 500,000 TEUs at risk. Talks between the Pacific Maritime Association and ILWU Local 26 reached an impasse on Tuesday, with the PMA saying there had been little or no movement from the union. The watchmen, who handle gate security and cargo watch, voted to authorise a strike in late October, and talks have been extended three times. Other longshore workers are expected to honour a picket line. The apparel and footwear trade is particularly exposed, since the Los Angeles district handled 49% of US footwear imports by value in 2025. Rail congestion is already heavy, with over 20,000 containers waiting at each port, and retailers are concerned about Black Friday deliveries.

Experts also flagged that most faux fur is synthetic and sheds microplastics.

stories.claim: New UK criminal offences on strangulation and certain pornography took effect this month in England and Wales, with enforcement questions open.
stories.summary: New criminal offences in England and Wales now make it illegal to possess or publish certain pornography, including material depicting strangulation or suffocation, sexual activity between apparent relatives, and activity involving someone who appears to be under 16. The changes came into force this month as part of the government's target to cut combined rates of domestic abuse, sexual assault and stalking by 50% within a decade. Campaigners welcomed the step, but questions remain over enforcement, the scope of the law and whether platforms will be required to remove such content. Baroness Gabby Bertin, who led the 2025 Independent Pornography Review, said the law brings online material closer to offline rules. Police and the Crown Prosecution Service will decide which acts are prohibited, and there are no routine device checks planned.

stories.claim: About 1,500 jobs are at risk at David Jones as its 19 closing stores face cuts after the collapse into administration.
stories.summary: Australia's oldest department store chain, David Jones, is cutting around 1,500 jobs across 19 stores slated for closure after entering voluntary administration on 5 November. The union SDA says only 170 of the 1,689 affected store workers have been offered redeployment, and half the roles are casual staff with no entitlements to be paid out on closure. Administrators McGrathNicol say the retailer owes at least A$459 million to creditors, including A$11 million owed to about 6,242 employees. The company plans to close 18 of its 37 Australian stores and one in New Zealand by year-end, and administrators have contacted 150 potential buyers. Bloomberg reports that several large firms are discussing hiring some of the affected workers, with further talks planned for early next week.

stories.headline: PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here
stories.claim: PHP 8.6 released with stricter security defaults, patches for seven critical RCE flaws, and new language features.
stories.summary: PHP 8.6 shipped on Thursday with security defaults tightened after a month of intense scrutiny over a swarm of vulnerabilities. Coordinated patch releases (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36) closed seven critical remote code execution flaws that had exposed applications such as WordPress, Laravel and Symfony. The new version stops PHP accepting session IDs it did not create, makes null-byte strings throw errors instead of being silently truncated, and makes some file functions return false on failure. It also adds partial function application, a native polling API, a Duration class and clamp(). Administrators may gain little, however, because configuration files that override the defaults will keep the old, looser behaviour.
key_points: PHP 8.6 was released on Thursday, alongside patched 8.5, 8.4, 8.3 and 8.2 branches that fixed seven critical RCE flaws.
Strict Mode now rejects uninitialised session IDs, blocking a session-fixation trick that enabled hijacking and CSRF.
Null-byte strings now trigger errors more often, closing a common route for remote code execution.
New features include partial function application, a native polling API, a Duration class spanning over 250 years, and clamp().
Existing php.ini or framework settings can override the new defaults, so many deployments may not benefit until they change configuration.
